title: What Really Happens to Your Recycling After the Truck
summary: Follow one recycling bin through a material recovery facility: hand sorting, disc screens, magnets, eddy currents, optical sorters and the baler. Then see why some of it is turned away, what changed when China restricted scrap imports in 2018, and the real recycling numbers by material in the US and Canada.
sources: Corrugated boxes recycled at 96.5% in 2018; aluminum beverage cans 50.4% (670,000 tons); glass containers 31.3% (3.1 million tons); PET bottles and jars 29.1%; plastic containers and packaging 13.6% (US EPA, Containers and Packaging: Product-Specific Data, 2018 data): https://www.epa.gov/facts-and-figures-about-materials-waste-and-recycling/containers-and-packaging-product-specific

Plastics generation 35.7 million tons in 2018; about three million tons recycled, an 8.7 percent recycling rate; 27 million tons landfilled (US EPA, Plastics: Material-Specific Data): https://www.epa.gov/facts-and-figures-about-materials-waste-and-recycling/plastics-material-specific-data

292.4 million tons of municipal solid waste generated in 2018; about 69 million tons recycled and 25 million tons composted, a 32.1% recycling and composting rate; data current through 2018 (US EPA, National Overview: Facts and Figures on Materials, Wastes and Recycling): https://www.epa.gov/facts-and-figures-about-materials-waste-and-recycling/national-overview-facts-and-figures-materials

Much of the material collected in recycling programs is directed to about 500 MRFs; contamination, the amount of nonrecyclables collected curbside, is 15-20 percent on average; a typical MRF captures about 87 percent of its incoming accepted program recyclable materials (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Municipal Solid Waste Recycling in the United States: Analysis of Current and Alternative Approaches, 2025, ch. 2): https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/27978/chapter/4

How a material recovery facility sorts a blue cart: trucks unload, workers pre-sort plastic bags and hazardous items by hand, disc screens lift cardboard and flat paper, a glass breaker shatters glass so it falls through a screen and a cyclone lifts lighter paper and plastic off it, optical sorters with air jets, a magnet picks up tin cans, an eddy current 'acts like a magnet in reverse' and repels foil, cans and pie plates onto another belt, sorted material is baled and sold; '90% automated sorting by machines', 'the other 10% is handled manually'; 'garbage bags are never opened during the sorting process'; destinations: plastics to Canada, metal cans and foil to Eastern Canada, cardboard to Canada and the US, paper to Eastern Canada, the US, India, Malaysia and Taiwan, glass to Western Canada (City of Calgary, How the recycling facility works): https://www.calgary.ca/uep/wrs/recycling-information/residential-services/blue-cart-recycling/how-recycling-works.html

WTO notification G/TBT/N/CHN/1211, 18 July 2017: Catalogue of Solid Wastes Forbidden to Import into China by the End of 2017 (4 classes, 24 kinds), including plastic scrap, mixed paper waste, textile waste and vanadium slag (WTO TBT notification; copy hosted by UNEP): https://apps1.unep.org/resolutions/uploads/2017-world_trade_organization-chn1211_1.pdf

China's policies, initially implemented in January 2018, include bans on mixed paper and contaminant limits of 0.5 percent on old corrugated containers and old newspapers; US exports to China of mixed paper decreased by 98.8 percent from Q1 2017 (575.6 thousand metric tons) to Q1 2019 (6.7 thousand metric tons); India and Indonesia partially filled the gap (US International Trade Commission, Executive Briefing on Trade, Nov 2019, S. Scott and R. Ireland): https://www.usitc.gov/publications/332/executive_briefings/ebot_trade_in_wastepaper.pdf

In 2022, 27.1% of solid waste generated in Canada was diverted and 72.9% sent for disposal (9.9 of 36.5 million tonnes); paper 3.571 million tonnes of diverted material; over 3 million tonnes of plastic are thrown away by Canadians each year but only 9% get diverted (Environment and Climate Change Canada, Solid waste diversion and disposal indicator, updated 28 Nov 2024): https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/solid-waste-diversion-disposal.htm

9.9 million tonnes of waste diverted in Canada in 2022; paper fibres up to 3.6 million tonnes, more than one-third of all diverted materials (Statistics Canada, StatsCAN Plus, Less diversion and more non-residential sources push Canada's waste disposal to new high in 2022): https://statcan.gc.ca/o1/en/plus/6850-less-diversion-and-more-non-residential-sources-push-canadas-waste-disposal-new-high-2022

scenes.narration: {96.5%|Ninety-six and a half percent} of US cardboard boxes get recycled.
Count every kind of plastic, and it's {8.7%|eight point seven percent}.
So what really happens to your recycling after the truck pulls away?
In {2018|twenty eighteen}, one country's new rules showed who really decides what gets recycled.
By the end, you'll know how one bin gets sorted, why some of it gets turned away, and who really decides.
Part one: the sort.
Follow one bin. The truck dumps it at a sorting plant called a material recovery facility.
Much of America's recycling goes to about {500|five hundred} of these plants.
First, people. Workers pull out plastic bags and anything dangerous, by hand.
Then machines. Big cardboard rides over spinning discs, and smaller things fall through.
Glass gets broken on purpose, so the pieces drop through a screen.
Cameras spot each kind of paper and plastic. A puff of air knocks it onto its own line.
A magnet lifts the steel cans out.
Aluminum gets the opposite: an eddy current, a magnet in reverse, that kicks cans and foil onto another belt.

data.label: EDDY CURRENT
data.source: CITY OF CALGARY · HOW IT WORKS

scenes.narration: Machines do about {90%|ninety percent} of the sorting. People handle the other {10%|ten}.

data.label: BY MACHINE
data.source: CITY OF CALGARY · HOW IT WORKS

scenes.narration: Last stop: the baler. Each material gets pressed into a square bale, stacked and sold.
If you like seeing where things really go, subscribe. A new system every Sunday.
Part two: the rejects.
Not everything that rides the truck is on the plant's list.
On average, {15 to 20%|fifteen to twenty percent} of what's collected at the curb can't be recycled there at all.
And for the workers' safety, a tied garbage bag is never opened. Whatever's inside goes to landfill.
Good material slips past too. A typical plant captures about {87%|eighty-seven percent} of the recyclables it accepts.
But the real test comes after the plant. A bale only gets recycled if somebody buys it.
Part three: the buyers.
Bales are raw material. Calgary's cardboard goes to mills in Canada and the US. Its paper travels as far as India, Malaysia and Taiwan.

data.label: AS RAW MATERIAL
data.source: CITY OF CALGARY · WHERE IT GOES

scenes.narration: And buyers can change the rules. In July {2017|twenty seventeen}, China told the World Trade Organization it would ban {24|twenty-four} kinds of solid waste, including plastic scrap and mixed paper.
What it still took, like cardboard and newspaper, could hold at most {0.5%|half a percent} contamination.
In two years, American mixed paper shipped to China fell {98.8%|ninety-eight point eight percent}. India and Indonesia took some of it.
So what really decides? Not your bin, and not the machines. The buyer of the bale.
Here's how that adds up in the US. Boxes, {96.5%|ninety-six and a half percent}. Aluminum cans, about half. Glass containers, {31%|thirty-one}. Plastic bottles, {29%|twenty-nine}.
Across all US trash, {32.1%|thirty-two point one percent} was recycled or composted in {2018|twenty eighteen}.
Canada counts diversion, compost included: {27.1%|twenty-seven point one percent} in {2022|twenty twenty-two}.
And plastic? {8.7%|Eight point seven percent} in the US. About {9%|nine percent} diverted in Canada.
So after the truck, your bin gets screened, scanned, pulled, pushed and baled. Then it waits for a buyer. Boxes almost always find one.
